items.title: Show HN: Acyclic; Rapid agent swarms
items.summary: Hi HN, we're the co-founders of Acyclic (YC F26). Acyclic runs any agentic workflow as a swarm. You give it a task and your project; it splits the work across many coding agents, each in its own sandbox, runs them in parallel, and merges what they produce into one patch or pull request. Our thesis: agentic workflows should be realtime, no matter how complex the task. The bottleneck should be human ideation and design, whilst building happens at the speed of thought. To bring this to you we make our agents recursively fork and speculative execute. This means that if an agent has 2 independent tasks to do, it will just split into 2 agents to solve both tasks quickly and merge back up the tree. Additionally, for sequential operations we have “speculative” agents which guess the next steps of the workflow as a pre-fetch step. To make this efficient we are solving the infrastructure bottlenecks. We are solving the memory, communication, routing and durable execution issues. This infra is open source at acyclic.dev/github, so check it out! To run your own swarm (check out acyclic.dev for a full guide) ``` npm install -g @acyclic-labs/cli acyclic swarm run --task <prompt> --dir <files_to_upload> ``` A good (non-coding) first task to try out: Do deep research into a person. “Do deep research into Jeff Goldblum“ You can view the results at acyclic.dev/dashboard or stream the results back to the cli using: ``` acyclic swarm pull <swarm-id> --apply ``` Check out some more research examples at acyclic.dev/evals, right now our biggest useful swarm is 236 agents for a code migration.

Show HN: KiviDB, a faster Redis-compatible memory database and vector cache
items.summary: Hi all, So I have been working on this project KiviDB from February 2026. It started as a project for me to understand rust, having a product with no GC pauses, memory blow up after snapshots and getting OOM on running pods, and that was actually an issue I faced with Dragonfly. I wanted to have something picking the best of Rust, but also picking the best parts of other alternatives like Garnet and Dragonfly. I used AI a lot, but I was the one making the design decisions based on the tests that claude picked from my history of troubleshooting sessions as part of my job. KiviDB supports both RESP2 and RESP3 protocol. I had some founders credits on my AWS account which helped me with the infra, and running instances I could perform benchmark on. Its keyspace is sharded across threads, it is multi-threaded in nature, and performs best on Linux due to io_uring, I used the tokio_uring crate for this. It also has tokio fallback for other OS's. I hadn't open sourced it until recently as I felt it was not ready yet, the best way to learn it was to build a cloud managed service for it across all three widely used cloud providers i.e AWS, GCP and azure. Since I used to mainly work with cloud, I had some insights on what would be the best ways for the deployments, how to conduct failovers, manage SLAs, etc. And that's what I took help from claude to fast pace it. The website does look like AI slop but it works for now, given my limited resources, that's all I had. You may check it out at : https://kividb.io , I open sourced the core engine under AGPLv3, didn't want to have just source available, because that is available with other tools too. It supports apprx 98-99% of the redis 8.10 commands, few have issues and you can find them at https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/issues , contributors are welcome. Now the numbers, for the final benchmark, I used 2 c7gn.metal servers, in the same placement group in us-east1, and I used memtier-benchmark tool for this. The setting was : 10M keys, 100B each, 32 cores in use with both pipeline and un-pipelined runs. pipeline 16 GET: KiviDB 21.2M ops/sec vs Dragonfly 2.0 9.1M, Redis 8.10 2.4M, Redis Cluster 32 shards 4.7M When not pipelined, Dragonfly performed slightly better at 3.35M ops/sec vs kividb at 3.07M ops/sec. Memory per key was also slightly worse than dragonfly and almost same as Redis, 177B (kividb) vs 134B (dragonfly) vs 178B (redis). With vector ingestion times it was slower but when querying, it was faster than most alternatives at lower ef, however slower than dragonfly at high ef. Most of the technical details are mentioned here so you can check it out: https://kividb.io/benchmarks . easiest way to try it: docker run -d -p 6380:6380 kividb/kividb I am looking forward to building a community around this, provide better rust based tools, I am open to constructive criticism and value informed opinion. Thanks

items.title: Show HN: ApolloOffice – Local AI workers that turn GitHub issues into tested PRs
items.summary: This is a little thing I built: it's a visually pleasing office with AI agents working on GitHub repositories and submitting pull requests. They are getting issues, reproduce them and then fix them. I was using it privately in a Discord call and many people requested a public open-source version, so I got Claude Opus 5.5 to rewrite the entire code in Rust. It's available as a service on macOS, Linux and Windows. In my use case I use it to make PRs for ArtCraft, the Adobe Suite clone that is viral right now. This tool got me into the top 10 contributors within 5 days. I have 361 total pull requests, 234 of them got merged. I think that statistic speaks for the quality this thing can achieve. Right now on low usage settings it's round about 51 pulls a day fast, and it does not use up as much usage as you think it would, mainly because the tasks get split between Haiku models on default settings and not everything is running on one big Opus session. Also they get optimal prompts and clear instructions every step, which further reduces token usage. It can also bughunt: about 60% of pulls are code problems the tool found by itself. If you are a GitHub contributor to any project or want to solve issues on your own repository, this is the tool for you.

items.summary: 0sql is an open-source semantic layer engine written in Rust. Compared to Cube and Metricflow, here are the major differences: Partition aware, agg aware, and compute engine aware semantic routing. Comprehensive suite of measures out of the box. Snapshot, LOD, compound, ratios, calculations, cross-domain, and run time measure transformations. Automatic data blending across fact domains. Row level security built-in.
